extracted.intended_audience: translators of classical Latin poetry; literary translators working on Horace
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for producing an English poetic translation of Horace's Satires and Epistles, covering metre, style, handling of local/temporary allusions, fidelity vs freedom, and selection/omission of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The measure in which Horace may best be represented is the heroic of ten syllables (the English heroic couplet) rather than the Hudibrastic octosyllabic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the octosyllabic (Hudibrastic) is colloquial and apt to become slipshod or unclassical; English heroic couplet can represent changes of mood in Horace's hexameter and is the recognized metre of English satire. Beware using a shorter colloquial metre consistently only for some poems — consistency with the Latin is preferable. (Text: "the measure in which Horace may best be represented is the heroic ... of ten syllables."; critique of octosyllabic follows.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of metrical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw an English metrical line where none exists in the Latin; apply metre consistently across Horace's hexameter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator should avoid making arbitrary metrical distinctions among Horace's hexameter poems (e.g., using different metres for 'light' vs 'grave' pieces) because Horace himself does not draw such a line. (Text: "To draw a metrical line in the English where none is drawn in the Latin appears to me objectionable ipso facto ...")

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and idiom for heroic metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Cowper as the primary English model for the heroic couplet applied to Horace, borrowing occasional graces from Pope where helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cowper provides ease and terseness in metre and style suited to Horace; Pope's terseness is different (trimness and antithetical smartness). While Cowper is the right model, borrow selectively from others for grace. Beware that an inferior workman handling Cowper's manner may become flat or insipid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiomatic, conversational style
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to follow the ordinary language of good society — conversation and familiar letter-writing — rather than elevated poetic diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace's persiflage and colloquial manner are best rendered by idiomatic prosaic ring in English. Colloquial abbreviations may be used freely where appropriate. Avoid being a minute purist on grammar; prefer idiomatic speech that reflects the original's ease. (Text: "... try to follow the ordinary language of good society ... the language of conversation and of familiar letter-writing.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation must proceed on the principle of compensation: losses in one place may be recovered elsewhere so that the general effect of the whole resembles the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on reproducing the general effect of sentences/paragraphs rather than strict line-by-line fidelity. Small added liveliness or sharpened points in English can compensate for inevitable losses. (Includes Johnson quote: 'It is not by comparing line with line that the merit of works is to be estimated, but by their general effects and ultimate result.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the author's manner and individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority is to reproduce Horace's manner (ease, terseness, persiflage, individuality) rather than literal wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator risks losing all charm or missing Horace's individuality if they render him too literally or change his manner. Where Horace rises in tone, the translator should attempt to rise; for the greater part, aim to 'creep along the ground.' Avoid making the author vulgar or flat as many earlier translators did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epigrammatic additions sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional small epigrammatic or pungent additions are acceptable to supply what is effective in Latin but would read as insipid in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such additions should be minor, made in full confidence that trifling liveliness compensates for heavier unavoidable losses. Don't consciously depart from the spirit of the original. (Footnote quoting Cowper: sometimes the 'turn' must be supplied in English.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling local and temporary allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Three permissible approaches: translate verbally (risking unintelligibility), generalize special references, or introduce a modern equivalent/imitator's licence — the last to be used very sparingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator should prefer to employ the three courses as needed, using modern equivalents only for very minor points (examples: turning a scarus into a sardine; converting sestertia into an English sum roughly equivalent). Avoid wholesale transformation of ancient particulars into modern specifics (e.g., Dryden-style anachronisms). The goal is to lay open ancient life without wantonly sacrificing antique spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal paraphrase for omitted passages
rubrics_metrics.description: When omitting entire satires or passages (because they cannot be rendered without offence), do not generally paraphrase the omitted matter — stay silent instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator may omit material unsuited to modern sensibilities; but avoid paraphrasing what is left out. The translator should include in notes where indebtedness to predecessors exists, but otherwise refrain from substituting paraphrase for omitted text. (Text: 'Where I have not translated I have not in general cared to paraphrase, but have been silent altogether.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive literalness; take latitude where necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the main characteristic of the original is ease, the translator must take considerable latitude rather than translate irrespectively of English idiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bear the Latin in mind, but accept departing from literal wording if needed to preserve ease and idiomatic quality in English. Study commentators but do not be slavish to previous translations; consult predecessors only after making own translation of a passage. (Text: 'Taken altogether, this translation will be found less close to the original than those with which I have formerly troubled the public.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone-management: rise where the original rises
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to match shifts of tone: when Horace 'rises' (more serious/elevated), the translator should attempt a corresponding rise; otherwise aim for a mainly prosaic/colloquial tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Where Horace evidently means to rise, I have attempted to rise too: but through the greater part of this work I have been anxious ... to creep along the ground.' Accept risk of occasional triviality or pertness but prefer idiomatic modesty to misplaced poetical ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice about rendering numerical/currency specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Render Roman sums/objects into English equivalents only where helpful and usually in a roughly equivalent manner; arbitrariness for context/metre is allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator may convert sestertia into English sums (e.g., dozens/hundreds of pounds) when it suits context or metre, but should avoid gratuitous distortion of antique reality. Small pragmatic changes acceptable to help modern readers or meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity in what to translate
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate the parts a 'well-judging reader would wish to dwell on' and omit parts that no one would now wish to see translated or that would be offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The translator has discretion to omit entire satires or passages; this selection should aim to present what will be of value to modern readers and reflect 'the broad features of Roman life' without gratuitous offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prior translations and scholarship judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult previous translations and commentators but avoid early dependence; acknowledge conscious debts in notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator should avoid consulting predecessors on a passage until after producing his own translation to prevent uncritical imitation. Where indebtedness occurs, cite it in notes. Study commentators to inform choices without surrendering original judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for 'plainness' rather than forced poetical ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a general quality of plainness—an idiomatic prosaic ring—preferring simple, natural expression over poetical elaboration where the original is colloquial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject renderings that are 'poetical' in a way unsuited to Horace's idiom; prefer expressions that have a prosaic ring while avoiding feebleness. This may require deliberately rejecting a graceful rendering in favor of idiomatic plainness.
